bottleneck: We can synthesize and edit genomes, but we cannot reliably predict what a novel genome will do once booted in a cell. Epistasis, regulatory logic, and cellular context mean designed sequences behave differently than models predict, forcing slow design-build-test cycles with high failure rates. Even small changes can have system-wide effects through feedback loops that no model captures. This unpredictability is the core reason synthetic biology is still closer to craft than to engineering, despite decades of progress.
current_state: AI-assisted design and automated biofoundries are accelerating iteration from years to months, but first-pass success for complex synthetic systems remains rare. Most designs still require multiple empirical debugging rounds.
title: Synthetic genome behavior resists prediction
why_it_blocks: Engineering requires predictable parts, and biology does not yet supply them. Until designed genomes behave as modeled, every synthetic organism demands expensive empirical debugging, keeping costs high and timelines long for biomanufacturing and therapeutics.
